lead: On a Friday of Qyomtho the Church remembers the Passion in the light of the empty tomb. Hebrews explains the death of Christ as the blood of a new covenant, sealing God's promise as Moses once sealed the covenant at Sinai. Luke shows Jesus at a meal, telling guests to take the lowest place and hosts to invite those who cannot repay. The one who took the lowest place on the Cross is the host of the new covenant's table. The key words are covenant, blood and lowest place.

r.h: The mediator of a new covenant
set: Chapters 8–10 of Hebrews compare the worship of the first covenant with the work of Christ. Chapter 8 quoted at length Jeremiah's promise of a new covenant (Jeremiah 31:31–34). In 9:1–14 the writer described the tent of the old worship and the Day of Atonement, and said that Christ entered the true sanctuary “with his own blood” (9:12).
Today's verses explain why a death was needed. The writer uses the fact that one Greek word can mean both “covenant” and “will”, and then recalls the covenant ceremony at Sinai (Exodus 24:3–8).
str: v. 15: Christ the mediator; his death redeems.
vv. 16–17: a will takes effect only at death.
vv. 18–21: the first covenant was also sealed with blood.
v. 22: no forgiveness without the shedding of blood.
kw: In the Greek Old Testament this word translates the Hebrew bᵉrît, covenant. In ordinary Greek it meant a last will. Hebrews plays on both: God's promises come to us as an inheritance through the death of the Son.
One who stands between two parties and brings them together. Christ is mediator because he is both God and man (1 Timothy 2:5).
A word not found in any earlier Greek writing known to us. Behind it lies the teaching of Leviticus that “the life of the flesh is in the blood” (Leviticus 17:11): blood offered means life given.
vv: For this reason he is the mediator of a new covenant, so that those who are called may receive the promised eternal inheritance,
The goal is not only the removal of sin but an inheritance. Those who are called become heirs.
Hence not even the first covenant was inaugurated without blood.
At Sinai, half the blood was thrown on the altar and half on the people (Exodus 24:6–8). God and people were bound together in one life.
This is the blood of the covenant that God has ordained for you.
Moses said “See the blood of the covenant” (Exodus 24:8). The form Hebrews gives, “This is”, is close to the Lord's words over the cup at the Supper (Mark 14:24).
without the shedding of blood there is no forgiveness of sins.
The writer states the principle of the old worship in order to show its fulfilment. The blood of animals pointed to the one gift of life that truly takes sin away.
ch: The Catechism teaches that the sacrifice of Christ is the sacrifice of the New Covenant, which restores us to communion with God through “the blood of the covenant” poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins (CCC 613). In the Holy Qurbono the priest repeats the Lord's words over the cup, and the Church receives the blood of the new covenant as her Lord commanded.

r.h: Take the lowest place; invite the poor
set: Jesus has gone on a sabbath to eat at the house of a leader of the Pharisees (14:1). He accepts the hospitality of Pharisees more than once in Luke (7:36; 11:37), and they are watching him closely. At such dinners guests reclined on couches arranged around the table, and the places nearest the host were the places of honour.
Jesus speaks first to the guests (vv. 7–11) and then to the host (vv. 12–14). What sounds like advice on manners is a parable about the kingdom.
str: vv. 7–11: to the guests: do not seek the first place.
vv. 12–14: to the host: invite those who cannot repay.
kw: Literally “first couch”. Seeking it was a way of claiming status in front of others.
The saying in v. 11 uses passives, “will be humbled”, “will be exalted”. It is God who does the lifting, as Mary sings: he “lifted up the lowly” (Luke 1:52).
The same root appears for repayment at the resurrection. God himself becomes the one who repays those who gave without return.
vv: When he noticed how the guests chose the places of honor, he told them a parable.
Luke calls it a parable. The table is an image of God's kingdom, where places are given, not grabbed.
For all who exalt themselves will be humbled, and those who humble themselves will be exalted.
Jesus says it again after the parable of the Pharisee and the tax collector (18:14). He lived it first, by taking the lowest place of all on the Cross.
But when you give a banquet, invite the poor, the crippled, the lame, and the blind.
These are the very people the master brings in at the great dinner a few verses later (14:21).
for you will be repaid at the resurrection of the righteous.
Generosity that expects nothing in return is a sign of faith in the resurrection. We give now because we believe God will answer later.
ch: The Church reads this teaching as part of her preferential love for the poor. The Catechism says that God blesses those who come to the aid of the poor (CCC 2443), and that love for the poor belongs to the constant tradition of the Church (CCC 2444). Every gathering of Christians, from the parish feast to the family table, is measured by this Gospel.

study: Hebrews calls Christ's death the beginning of an inheritance. What does it mean to me that I am an heir of God's promises?
Whom could I invite, or help, this week who cannot repay me?
